summary: A major Western European power; the French Revolution and Enlightenment thought have had a profound influence on the modern world, and France is known for art, fashion, wine and cuisine, with “the gastronomic meal of the French” inscribed on UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural Heritage list.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: French secularization has deep historical roots: the Revolution of 1789 confiscated church property and promoted “dechristianization,” in the 19th century republicans and the Catholic Church were long opposed, and the 1905 law on the Separation of the Churches and the State established the principle of “laïcité” (secularism), under which the state neither recognizes nor funds any religion. The social changes and urbanization after the 1960s sharply reduced church attendance, and today more than half of the French identify as non-religious.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Between about 496 and 508 the Frankish king Clovis was baptized, and France was therefore called the “eldest daughter of the Church.” After the Wars of Religion of the 16th century (1562–1598) and Louis XIV’s revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685, which drove out the Protestants, Catholicism became overwhelmingly dominant. After the Revolution Napoleon signed a concordat with the papacy in 1801, but after the separation of church and state in 1905 the Church lost its official status, and today most Catholics enter a church only for baptisms, weddings and funerals.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: France ruled Algeria from 1830 to 1962 and controlled Morocco and Tunisia. Postwar reconstruction in the 1950s–70s required large numbers of workers, and North African laborers moved in en masse and, after 1976, settled through family reunification, giving France the largest Muslim community in Western Europe, concentrated in the suburbs around Paris, Lyon and Marseille. The 2004 law banning students from wearing headscarves and other religious symbols in public schools shows the tension between Islam and secularism.

ranking.name: Other Christian (Protestant, Orthodox, etc.)
ranking.description: Protestantism (the Huguenots) expanded rapidly in the 16th century; the Edict of Nantes of 1598 granted freedom of worship, and after its revocation in 1685 large numbers of believers fled abroad; today Protestants are concentrated in Alsace and the Cévennes, and in recent years evangelical churches of African immigrants have also grown rapidly. Orthodoxy comes mainly from exiles after the Russian Revolution of 1917 and from Armenian refugees after 1915.

ranking.name: Judaism
ranking.description: Jews have lived in Gaul since Roman times, and in 1791 France became the first country in Europe to grant Jews full citizenship. The Dreyfus affair of 1894 exposed anti-Semitism, and during World War II more than seventy thousand Jews were deported to concentration camps. After Algeria’s independence in 1962 large numbers of North African Jews moved in, so France today has the largest Jewish community in Europe.

religion.background: In the Middle Ages France was a core Catholic country, and the Wars of Religion in the 16th century and the expulsion of the Protestants in 1685 established the exclusive dominance of Catholicism. The Revolution of 1789 delivered a violent blow to the power of the Church, and the 19th-century struggle between republicans and the Church finally led to the 1905 separation law, with secularism becoming a core value of the French Republic. In the late 20th century France secularized rapidly, while historical ties with the North African colonies brought large numbers of Muslim immigrants, making the relationship between religion and secularism an important issue in contemporary France.

ranking.name: French
ranking.description: French developed from the Vulgar Latin of Gaul and was influenced by the Germanic language of the Franks; the Oaths of Strasbourg of 842 are among the earliest French documents. In 1539 Francis I issued the Ordinance of Villers-Cotterêts, requiring legal documents to use French rather than Latin; in 1635 the Académie française was founded to regulate the language. During the Revolution the government saw dialects as an obstacle to unity, and only after Ferry introduced free compulsory education in the 1880s did French become the mother tongue of the whole population.

ranking.name: Arabic (North African dialects)
ranking.description: The colonial relationship between France and North Africa lasted more than a hundred years; from the 1950s large numbers of Algerian, Moroccan and Tunisian workers came to France, and after Algeria’s independence in 1962 the pro-French “Harkis” and their families also moved in. Their families still speak North African Arabic dialects, while the second and third generations mostly use French as their main language, but many North African words have entered the slang of French young people.

ranking.name: Regional languages (Occitan, Breton, Alsatian, etc.)
ranking.description: Regional languages such as Occitan (southern France), Breton (northwest, a Celtic language) and Alsatian (northeast, a Germanic language) were once the mother tongues of many local residents. From the late 19th century schools strictly forbade pupils to speak dialects, and those caught had to wear a punishment token, causing these languages to decline rapidly in the twentieth century. From 1977 Breton-language immersion schools appeared, and a 2008 constitutional amendment recognized regional languages as part of France’s heritage, but speakers are still mostly elderly.

language.history: After Rome conquered Gaul, Latin replaced Celtic, and after the Franks took over in the 5th century, the “langue d’oïl” in the north and the “langue d’oc” in the south gradually diverged. The expansion of royal power centered on Paris made the northern dialect the basis of French, which became the language of administration from 1539; in the 17th century the Académie française set norms, and French became the language of European courts and diplomacy. The Revolution and the national education of the Third Republic promoted linguistic unification, causing regional languages to decline; in the late 20th century immigrants brought new languages such as Arabic, and regional-language preservation movements also gradually arose.

ranking.name: Baguette
ranking.description: A long, thin bread made from flour, water, salt and yeast, with a golden crisp crust and a soft, chewy interior with large holes; it is the staple French people buy every day.
ranking.history: The development of the baguette is related to the spread of steam ovens in the 19th century, and in 1839 the Austrian August Zang opened the “Boulangerie Viennoise” in Paris, bringing new baking techniques. A common account holds that in 1920 France banned bakers from working before four in the morning, which pushed them to make a thin loaf with a shorter baking time. In 1993 the French government set by decree that the “traditional French baguette” may use only flour, water, salt and yeast, and in 2022 the artisanal know-how and culture of the baguette was inscribed on UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural Heritage list; the French consume tens of millions of them every day.

ranking.name: Croissant
ranking.description: Dough is wrapped around butter, repeatedly rolled and folded, shaped into a crescent and baked, with a crisp, layered exterior and a soft interior with a rich butter aroma.
ranking.history: The ancestor of the croissant is the Austrian crescent-shaped bread “kipferl,” and after August Zang opened his Viennese bakery in Paris in 1839, Viennese-style pastries became fashionable in Paris. French bakers later switched to the technique of laminated butter dough, and in the early 20th century the method for the modern croissant began to appear in French recipes. The widely told story that it was invented to celebrate the defeat of the Ottomans during the Siege of Vienna in 1683 has no reliable evidence. Today the croissant and coffee are the classic image of a French breakfast.

ranking.name: Boeuf bourguignon
ranking.description: Chunks of beef are stewed for a long time with Burgundy red wine, onion, carrot and herbs, with bacon, mushrooms and pearl onions added, in a rich sauce.
ranking.history: Burgundy is famed for Charolais cattle and red wine, and this dish began as the home-style method of local farmers who stewed older, tougher beef in red wine for a long time until tender. In the 19th century it reached the tables of the Parisian bourgeoisie, and in the early 20th century the chef Escoffier included it in the classic French repertoire. In 1961 the American cook Julia Child introduced it in Mastering the Art of French Cooking and demonstrated it on television, making it one of the best-known French stews in the world.

ranking.name: Coq au vin
ranking.description: Chicken (traditionally a rooster) is first marinated in red wine, then stewed with bacon, mushrooms, pearl onions and herbs, in a deep red, thick sauce.
ranking.history: Coq au vin originated in the French countryside, and the traditional method uses an old rooster no longer suited for breeding, softening the meat through long stewing in wine, a piece of farmhouse wisdom about using everything. Folk tradition says it can be traced to the time of Caesar’s conquest of Gaul, but there is no reliable evidence, and actual recipes appear commonly in the literature only in the early 20th century. The rooster is one of the national symbols of France, and so this dish is often regarded as representative of traditional French country cooking.

ranking.name: Ratatouille
ranking.description: A vegetable dish stewed from tomato, eggplant, zucchini, sweet pepper and onion with olive oil and Provençal herbs, which can be eaten hot or cold.
ranking.history: Ratatouille originated around Nice in the south of France and is a home-style dish in which farmers stew together the abundant vegetables of summer. Tomatoes, peppers and zucchini are all native to the Americas or arrived relatively late, and became common in Provence only in the 18th–19th centuries, so the modern form of the dish is relatively young. The name is related to a verb for “to stir” in Occitan and French, and it originally referred to a coarse stew. The 2007 Pixar animated film Ratatouille made it famous around the world.
